title: Giving up touring: his wife's death and his own illness
summary: He stays home to nurse his sick wife, who dies in June 1966, then is hospitalised himself and goes to a rest home.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: No, I didn't go on no other trip at the time, because I called George and told him, I said, George, I think you're going to have to get another drummer, because my wife is very sick, and there's nobody but me to look after. So I'm going to have to call it off. I said, I'll play at the hall. I said, I'm freelancing. I said, I'll play with anybody that hires me. But I said, when they come down to making a trip anyway, I don't care if it's the Baton Rouge, Bugger Lou Sunday, I don't want to go out of town at the present time. That's why my wife is sick like she is. Well, he told me, all right, he wasn't angry or nothing about us, you know. Well, anyway, I stayed here and I looked after the best way I could, and I was still playing out there at the hall. Well, it had gotten so I had to put in the hospital. That was during the year of 1966, around Easter time. I put in there on a Friday before Palm Sunday, and she stayed in there until Good Friday. So Good Friday night, they brought her back in the ambulance. And I started taking care of her just the same as I was doing before. And all the neighbors there was getting kind of uneasy. I said, Mr. Joe, I said, you're beginning to look kind of very broke down running so much. I said, who else going to do it for me? I can't afford to pay nobody to run my errands. So naturally, I'll have to do them myself. So, on the 26th of June 1966, she died. 1966.

We buried on the 27th of June 1966. And it was during that time before she died that I started to take the seat. My legs had went bad on me. I used to have to use a chair to slide around on. You know, taking foot in this slide wherever I had to go to the bathroom. I had to slide in with the chair pulling along with me. So, I had gotten sold a week back then. Yeah, I was in the hospital about six weeks. I came out after July 4th. Must have been about a week after the 4th of July. Came home. I still couldn't do nothing for her. But I tried to get around the best way I could. But it looked like it was the hardest thing in the world for me to get enough appetite to eat. So, I called Jabber and I told him about it. He said, well, see the best thing for you to do is to go to a rest home. Maybe you need rest. I said, yeah, probably. So, I said, because I can't eat. I don't have an appetite. So, he said, well, we're going to take you to the rest home. So, sure enough, he came down the next morning early. He got me at them. Made arrangements for them up at the Hubbard home up in Carlton on Hamilton Street. And they brought me there. Well, that day they were serving oxtail stew. Well, I really enjoyed it. And they had greens with it. Well, his wife was with us and she told me, she said, Joe, now you eat all the greens you can. I said, I will. If that's going to help me, I'm going to do that. Well, I went in there on the last, the second, the last day of September of 1966. But I got so disgusted with the place. It was supposed to be somebody there that helped me to learn how to walk again. I didn't get that accommodation. I said, well, I can't stay here. I'm paying all this money. And all I'm getting is just three meals of there and they ain't worth a penny. I do better at home myself. So sure enough, I just got disgusted and left on the 15th of December of 1966. That was before my wife died. I came on home. I said, I got, I just, she wanted to find out. She asked me all kinds of questions. I said, I just want to go home. I said, I'm feeling better. I said, I just want to go home. So they released me. She got kind of angry. She said, well, you cannot get back in here no more. I said, I don't want to come back. I said, I'd much rather stay home and die if I can't do no better. So sure enough, a friend of mine, cab driver Pickle, came and got me, helped to bring me upstairs. And that's where I've been ever since. Outside the time I go out to the hall at, to the jam section. Cause I ain't been able to go out nowhere to buy no groceries or go shopping or nothing like that yet. Because my left leg is still kind of wobbly yet, you know.
